dsa-complexity:0.prompt: Linear search scans an unsorted array of n items for a target. What are its best-case and worst-case running times?
options: Best Θ(1), worst Θ(n)
Best Θ(n), worst Θ(n)
Best Θ(log n), worst Θ(n)
Best Θ(1), worst Θ(n log n)
dsa-complexity:0.explanation: If the target is the first element the search stops after one comparison (Θ(1)); if it is last or missing, all n items are checked (Θ(n)). Saying the best case is Θ(n) confuses 'the loop can run n times' with 'it always does'.

dsa-complexity:0.prompt: What is the time complexity of this function?
options: O(n log n)
O(n)
O(log^2 n)
dsa-complexity:0.explanation: The outer loop runs n times; the inner loop doubles j each time, so it runs about log2 n times. n × log n = O(n log n). It's not O(n^2) because the inner loop is not linear in n.

dsa-complexity:0.prompt: A quicksort implementation always picks the last element as the pivot. It is given an array that is already sorted. What happens?
options: It runs in Θ(n log n) because quicksort is n log n on average
It runs in Θ(n) because no swaps are needed
It degrades to Θ(n^2) because every partition is maximally unbalanced
It runs in Θ(log n) because the pivot is always the maximum
dsa-complexity:0.explanation: With the last element as pivot on sorted input, each partition splits off just one element, giving n + (n-1) + ... = Θ(n^2). The 'average' n log n assumes random-ish pivots; sorted input is exactly this pivot rule's worst case.

dsa-complexity:0.prompt: An algorithm's exact cost is T(n) = 3n^2 + 100·n·log n + 5. Which is the tightest correct description?
options: Θ(n log n), because the 100 coefficient dominates
Θ(n^3), as an upper bound
Θ(100 n log n + 3n^2)
dsa-complexity:0.explanation: For large n the n^2 term outgrows n log n regardless of constant factors, so T(n) = Θ(n^2). The 100 coefficient only matters for small n, and Θ notation drops constants and lower-order terms.

dsa-complexity:0.prompt: Which statement about insertion sort's running time is correct?
options: It is Θ(n^2) on every input because it has two nested loops
Its worst case is Θ(n^2) and its best case (already sorted) is Θ(n)
It is Θ(n log n) on average, like merge sort
Its best case is Θ(1) when the array is already sorted
dsa-complexity:0.explanation: On sorted input the inner loop exits immediately for each element, giving Θ(n); reverse-sorted input forces Θ(n^2) shifts. Nested loops don't imply Θ(n^2) on every input. Even the best case must look at all n elements, so it can't be Θ(1).
The inner loop runs 0+1+2+3+4 = n(n-1)/2 = 10 times. That is still Θ(n^2): halving the work of a full n×n loop changes the constant, not the growth rate. 15 would be n(n+1)/2, which counts j <= i.
i takes the values 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 (128 stops the loop), so 7 iterations, which is about ceil(log2 100). Loops that multiply the counter are logarithmic, not linear.

dsa-complexity:0.prompt: Which statements about asymptotic notation are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Big-Θ gives a tight bound: the function is bounded above and below by the same growth rate
Big-O can only be used to describe an algorithm's worst case
An O(n log n) algorithm can be slower than an O(n^2) one for small inputs
Any algorithm that must read its whole input is Ω(n)
Big-O keeps constant factors, so O(2n) and O(n) are different classes
dsa-complexity:0.explanation: Θ is a tight bound; constants hidden by Big-O can make an asymptotically better algorithm slower at small n; reading n items is a lower bound. Big-O is just an upper bound and can describe best, average or worst case. It drops constants, so O(2n) = O(n).

dsa-complexity:0.prompt: Which of these functions are O(n^2)? Select all that apply.
options: n log n
n^2 log n
dsa-complexity:0.explanation: Big-O is an upper bound, so anything growing no faster than n^2 qualifies: 5n^2+3n, n log n and 1000n. n^2 log n grows faster than n^2 by a log factor, and 2^n is exponential.

dsa-complexity:0.prompt: A hash table with average-case O(1) lookup guarantees that every single lookup finishes in constant time.
options: True
False
dsa-complexity:0.explanation: Average case is about typical inputs; with many collisions (bad hash function or adversarial keys) a lookup can degrade to O(n) for chaining. The guarantee is about the expected cost, not every operation.

dsa-complexity:0.prompt: A function that loops over an array of length n and then, separately (not nested), loops over another array of length m runs in O(n + m) time.
options: True
False
dsa-complexity:0.explanation: Sequential loops add their costs: O(n) + O(m) = O(n + m). Only nesting multiplies them (O(n·m)). Collapsing it to O(n) is wrong unless you know m is bounded by n.

dsa-complexity:1.prompt: You reverse an array in place by swapping arr[i] and arr[n-1-i] with two indices. What is the auxiliary space complexity?
options: O(n), because the array has n elements
O(log n)
O(n/2), because only half the elements are swapped
dsa-complexity:1.explanation: Auxiliary space counts extra memory beyond the input. Two indices and a temp variable are constant. The input array itself is O(n) but isn't counted as extra space for an in-place algorithm.

dsa-complexity:1.prompt: What is the space complexity of this function, including the call stack?
options: O(1), since no new arrays are created
O(n), because n stack frames are live at the deepest point
O(log n)
dsa-complexity:1.explanation: Each call waits for the next, so n frames are on the stack at once: O(n) space. 'No new arrays' misses the call stack, and JavaScript engines such as V8 do not perform tail-call optimisation.

dsa-complexity:1.prompt: A dynamic array grows by adding a fixed 10 slots each time it fills up, instead of doubling. What is the total cost of n pushes?
options: O(n) total, amortised O(1) per push
O(n log n) total
O(n^2) total, amortised O(n) per push
O(n) total, because 10 is a constant
dsa-complexity:1.explanation: Each resize copies all current elements: 10 + 20 + 30 + ... up to n is about n^2/20 copies, which is O(n^2). Amortised O(1) needs geometric growth (×1.5, ×2) so copy costs form a geometric series summing to O(n).

dsa-complexity:1.prompt: In a 'does any pair sum to target?' problem, the interviewer says memory is extremely tight but the array may be modified. Which approach fits best?
options: Store every value in a Set: O(n) time, O(n) space
Sort in place, then two pointers: O(n log n) time, O(1) extra space (ignoring sort internals)
Check all pairs: O(n^2) time, O(n) space
Build a frequency Map: O(n) time, O(1) space
dsa-complexity:1.explanation: Sorting in place plus two pointers trades some time for minimal extra memory. The Set approach is faster but uses O(n) space. Brute force needs only O(1) space, not O(n), but is slower, and a frequency map is O(n) space, not O(1).

dsa-complexity:1.prompt: How does amortised analysis differ from average-case analysis?
options: Amortised analysis averages over random inputs; average case averages over a sequence
Amortised analysis bounds the total cost of any sequence of operations, with no probability involved
They are the same thing with different names
Amortised analysis only applies to recursive algorithms
dsa-complexity:1.explanation: Amortised O(1) push means any sequence of n pushes costs O(n) total, a worst-case guarantee over the sequence. Average-case analysis assumes a distribution over inputs. Swapping the two definitions is the common mix-up.

dsa-complexity:1.prompt: This simulates a doubling dynamic array. What does it print?
dsa-complexity:1.explanation: Resizes happen when len is 1, 2, 4 and 8, copying 1+2+4+8 = 15 elements and ending at capacity 16. Total copies stay under n, which is why push is amortised O(1).

dsa-complexity:1.prompt: What does this print (max recursion depth, then total calls)?
dsa-complexity:1.explanation: Calls total 2^(n+1) - 1 = 31 (exponential time), but only one root-to-leaf path is on the stack at once, so the max depth is n + 1 = 5 (linear space). Time and space of recursion are governed by different things.

dsa-complexity:1.prompt: Which of these allocate O(n) extra memory for an array of length n? Select all that apply.
options: arr.slice()
[...arr].reverse()
arr.reverse()
new Set(arr)
Swapping elements with two index pointers
dsa-complexity:1.explanation: slice, spread and new Set all build a new collection of up to n entries. arr.reverse() mutates in place, and two-pointer swapping uses O(1) extra space.

dsa-complexity:1.prompt: Which statements about amortised O(1) push on a doubling array are correct? Select all that apply.
options: An individual push can cost O(n) when it triggers a resize
The bound holds for every sequence of n pushes, not just on average over random inputs
It means each push is O(1) with high probability
Growing by a factor of 1.5 instead of 2 still gives amortised O(1)
dsa-complexity:1.explanation: A resize push copies everything (O(n)), but the total over n pushes is O(n) for any sequence. Any constant growth factor above 1 gives a geometric series. There is no probability in amortised analysis.

dsa-complexity:1.prompt: An algorithm with O(1) space complexity uses no memory at all beyond its input.
options: True
False
dsa-complexity:1.explanation: O(1) space means the extra memory doesn't grow with n. It can still use a fixed number of variables, counters or even a fixed-size 26-slot array.

dsa-complexity:1.prompt: A standard top-down merge sort on arrays needs O(n) auxiliary space for merging.
options: True
False
dsa-complexity:1.explanation: Merging two sorted halves into a temporary buffer needs O(n) extra space (plus O(log n) stack). That's the usual trade-off versus heap sort, which sorts in O(1) extra space but isn't stable.

dsa-complexity:2.prompt: A BFS uses a plain array as its queue. On a graph with n nodes, what's the cost of the queue operations and the usual fix?
options: O(n) total; shift is O(1) like pop
O(n^2) worst case, because shift re-indexes the array; use a head index instead of shift
O(n log n), because shift is logarithmic
O(n^2), and the only fix is a linked-list library
dsa-complexity:2.explanation: Array.prototype.shift moves every remaining element down, so n shifts can cost O(n^2). Keeping a `head` index (read queue[head++]) makes dequeue O(1). You don't need a library for this.

dsa-complexity:2.prompt: You need to keep the items of array `a` (length n) that also appear in array `b` (length m). Which approach is asymptotically best?
options: a.filter(x => b.includes(x)): O(n + m)
const s = new Set(b); a.filter(x => s.has(x)): O(n + m) expected
a.filter(x => b.indexOf(x) !== -1): O(n log m)
Sort both and use includes: O(n log n)
dsa-complexity:2.explanation: Building a Set is O(m) and each has() is expected O(1), giving O(n + m). includes and indexOf are linear scans, so the filter versions are O(n·m), not O(n + m) or O(n log m).

dsa-complexity:2.prompt: What does the ECMAScript spec (since ES2019) together with V8's implementation guarantee about Array.prototype.sort?
options: Stable, O(n log n) worst case (V8 uses TimSort)
Unstable, O(n^2) worst case (V8 uses quicksort)
Stable only for arrays shorter than 10 elements
O(n) for numeric arrays because it uses radix sort
dsa-complexity:2.explanation: ES2019 requires sort to be stable, and V8 switched to TimSort, which is O(n log n) worst case and O(n) on already-sorted runs. The old V8 behaviour (insertion sort for short arrays, quicksort otherwise) was unstable.

dsa-complexity:2.prompt: A hot request path checks `Object.keys(cache).length > 1000` on a plain-object cache with k keys. What does that cost per call?
options: O(1), objects track their size
O(log k)
O(k), because it builds an array of all keys
O(1) amortised, because V8 caches the keys array
dsa-complexity:2.explanation: Object.keys allocates and fills a new array of all k keys on every call, so it's O(k) time and memory. A Map exposes `.size` in O(1), which is one reason to prefer Map for caches.

dsa-complexity:2.prompt: What is the expected time complexity of deduplicating an array with `[...new Set(arr)]`?
options: O(n log n)
O(n)
dsa-complexity:2.explanation: Each insertion into the Set is expected O(1) and spreading it back out is O(n), so the total is O(n) expected. O(n log n) would be the sort-then-dedupe approach.

dsa-complexity:2.prompt: What is the time complexity of this code for an array of n users?
options: O(n), reduce visits each element once
O(n log n)
O(n^2), because each step copies the whole accumulator
O(1) amortised per user
dsa-complexity:2.explanation: Spreading `acc` copies all keys collected so far, so step i costs O(i) and the total is O(n^2). Mutating the accumulator (acc[u.id] = u; return acc) or using a Map makes it O(n). Looping once doesn't make it O(n) if each step is O(n).

Without a comparator, sort converts elements to strings and compares UTF-16 code units, so '100' < '25' < '9'. Pass (a, b) => a - b for numeric order. The complexity is still O(n log n); only the order is surprising.

Sort is stable, so items with equal keys keep their original relative order: b before d (k = 1), a before c (k = 2), giving 'bdac'. Stability is what lets you sort by a secondary key first and the primary key second.

dsa-complexity:2.prompt: Which of these operations are O(1) (amortised or expected) in a modern engine such as V8? Select all that apply.
options: arr.push(x)
arr.pop()
arr.shift()
map.get(key)
arr.includes(x)
arr.length
dsa-complexity:2.explanation: push is amortised O(1), pop and length are O(1), and Map.get is expected O(1). shift re-indexes the remaining elements and includes scans linearly, so both are O(n).

dsa-complexity:2.prompt: Which of these are O(n) in the size of the array? Select all that apply.
options: arr.slice()
arr.at(-1)
new Set(arr)
arr.splice(0, 1)
arr.concat(other) (counting the copy of arr)
dsa-complexity:2.explanation: slice and concat copy elements, new Set inserts every element, and removing from the front with splice shifts everything left. at(-1) is a direct index access, which is O(1).

dsa-complexity:2.prompt: arr.pop() is O(n) because the engine has to re-index the remaining elements.
options: True
False
dsa-complexity:2.explanation: pop removes the last element, so no other indices change: it's O(1). Re-indexing happens with shift and unshift at the front, which is why those are O(n).

dsa-complexity:3.prompt: An interviewer asks you to reverse a string in place in JavaScript. What's the right response?
options: Swap str[i] and str[n-1-i] with two pointers
JS strings are immutable, so convert to an array, reverse it, and join (O(n) extra space)
Use str.reverse(), which mutates the string
Use str.replace with a regex to swap characters in place
dsa-complexity:3.explanation: Strings are immutable: assigning str[i] is silently ignored (or throws in strict mode). Two-pointer swapping is the right idea on a character array, not on a string. There's no String.prototype.reverse.

dsa-complexity:3.prompt: Move all zeros in an array to the end, keeping the order of the non-zero elements, in O(n) time and O(1) extra space. Which approach works?
options: Sort with a comparator that puts zeros last
Use a write index: copy each non-zero to arr[write++], then fill the rest with zeros
splice out each zero and push a zero at the end
Filter non-zeros into a new array and append zeros
dsa-complexity:3.explanation: One pass with a write pointer compacts the non-zeros in order, then the tail is zero-filled: O(n) time, O(1) space. splice in a loop is O(n^2), sorting is O(n log n), and filter uses O(n) extra space.

dsa-complexity:3.prompt: How do you rotate an array right by k positions in O(n) time and O(1) extra space?
options: Call arr.unshift(arr.pop()) k times
Reverse the whole array, then reverse the first k % n elements, then reverse the rest
Copy into a new array at index (i + k) % n
Sort the array by (index + k) % n
dsa-complexity:3.explanation: The triple-reverse trick is in place and touches each element a constant number of times. unshift is O(n) per call (O(n·k) overall), and copying to a new array is O(n) space. Remember k %= n for k > n.

dsa-complexity:3.prompt: Sort an array containing only 0s, 1s and 2s in a single pass with O(1) extra space. Which technique is this?
options: Counting sort with a Map
Dutch national flag: low, mid and high pointers
Merge sort
Binary search for each boundary
dsa-complexity:3.explanation: Dutch national flag keeps [0, low) as 0s, [low, mid) as 1s and (high, end] as 2s, swapping as mid advances. That's one pass in place. Counting sort is also O(n) but needs two passes.

dsa-complexity:3.prompt: This is supposed to remove every even number from the array in place. What's wrong?
options: Nothing: splice handles index shifting
After a splice, the next element slides into index i and gets skipped
splice can't be used inside a for loop
It runs forever because arr.length changes
dsa-complexity:3.explanation: Removing at i shifts the next element into i, then i++ skips it, so consecutive evens survive. Iterate backwards or use a write pointer. It also costs O(n^2) because each splice is O(n). It terminates since the length shrinks.
Reversing the whole array gives 7..1; reversing the first 3 gives 5,6,7; reversing the rest gives 1,2,3,4. Result: a right rotation by 3. 4,5,6,7,1,2,3 would be a left rotation.
Kadane's algorithm restarts the running sum whenever extending it is worse than starting fresh. The best subarray is [4, -1, 2, 1] = 6, found in one O(n) pass.

'l' has char code 108, and 108 - 97 = 11; it appears twice, so counts[11] is 2, and the first index holding 2 is also 11. A 26-slot array is a common O(1)-space alternative to a Map for lowercase letters.

dsa-complexity:3.prompt: Which of these array methods mutate the original array? Select all that apply.
options: sort()
toSorted()
splice()
slice()
reverse()
concat()
dsa-complexity:3.explanation: sort, splice and reverse change the array in place. toSorted (ES2023), slice and concat return new arrays. Mixing these up causes bugs when you sort an input the caller still relies on.

dsa-complexity:3.prompt: nums1 has length m + n, with m sorted values followed by n empty slots; nums2 has n sorted values. You merge nums2 into nums1 in place. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Filling from the back avoids overwriting nums1 values that haven't been compared yet
The merge runs in O(m + n) time
It needs O(m + n) extra space for a temporary buffer
Filling from the front works without shifting elements
dsa-complexity:3.explanation: Writing the largest remaining value into the last free slot never clobbers unread data, so the merge is O(m + n) time and O(1) extra space. Filling from the front would overwrite nums1's own values unless you shift them, which is O(m·n).

dsa-complexity:3.prompt: In JavaScript, `let s = 'cat'; s[0] = 'b';` changes s to 'bat'.
options: True
False
dsa-complexity:3.explanation: Strings are immutable primitives. The assignment is silently ignored in sloppy mode and throws a TypeError in strict mode. Build a new string or work on an array of characters instead.

dsa-complexity:4.prompt: Count the subarrays whose sum equals k in an array that may contain negative numbers. Which approach is O(n)?
options: A sliding window that shrinks when the sum exceeds k
Running prefix sum plus a Map counting how often each prefix sum has occurred
Sort the array, then use two pointers
Binary search on the prefix-sum array
dsa-complexity:4.explanation: A subarray (i, j] sums to k exactly when P[j] - P[i] = k, so at each j you add the count of earlier prefixes equal to P[j] - k. A sliding window needs non-negative values, and sorting destroys contiguity.

dsa-complexity:4.prompt: You build P with P[0] = 0 and P[i + 1] = P[i] + arr[i]. What is the sum of arr[l..r] inclusive?
options: P[r] - P[l]
dsa-complexity:4.explanation: P[r + 1] is the sum of arr[0..r] and P[l] is the sum of arr[0..l-1]; subtracting leaves arr[l..r]. P[r] - P[l] drops arr[r]: the classic off-by-one.

dsa-complexity:4.prompt: Why does the shrink-when-too-big sliding window fail for 'longest subarray with sum k' when the array has negative numbers, while prefix sums still work?
options: Sliding windows can't handle arrays longer than k
With negatives, the window sum isn't monotonic, so shrinking or growing doesn't reliably move it toward k
Prefix sums sort the array first, which removes negatives
Negative numbers overflow the window sum
dsa-complexity:4.explanation: A window relies on 'adding increases the sum, removing decreases it'. Negatives break that, so a window you discarded might have become valid. Prefix sums with a Map of first occurrences check every start point implicitly without that assumption.

dsa-complexity:4.prompt: With a 2D prefix sum S where S[i + 1][j + 1] is the sum of grid[0..i][0..j], what is the sum of the rectangle (r1, c1) to (r2, c2) inclusive?
dsa-complexity:4.explanation: Take the big rectangle, subtract the strip above and the strip to the left, then add back the top-left corner that was subtracted twice (inclusion–exclusion). Subtracting the corner a third time, or using unshifted indices, gives wrong sums.

dsa-complexity:4.prompt: An array of 10^5 values gets interleaved point updates and range-sum queries, about 10^5 of each. Why is a plain prefix-sum array a poor fit?
options: Prefix sums can't answer range queries on numbers larger than 2^31
Each update forces an O(n) rebuild of the prefix array, so a Fenwick tree or segment tree (O(log n) per op) fits better
Prefix sums need the array to be sorted after each update
Range queries become O(n) once any update happens
dsa-complexity:4.explanation: Changing arr[i] changes every P[j] for j > i, which is O(n) per update and about 10^10 operations here. A Fenwick or segment tree supports both updates and queries in O(log n). Queries on a prefix array would still be O(1) if it were rebuilt.
arr[2..5] = 4 + 1 + 5 + 9 = 19. P[6] = 23 and P[2] = 4, so 23 - 4 = 19. Using P[r] - P[l] would give 10 and drop the 9.
Prefix sums run 1, 3, 6, 3, 6. The matches are [1,2], [3], [1,2,3,-3], [3,-3,3] and the final [3], so 5. Seeding the map with {0: 1} is what counts subarrays that start at index 0.

dsa-complexity:4.prompt: This applies range increments with a difference array. What does it print?
dsa-complexity:4.explanation: Each update marks +v at l and -v at r + 1; a prefix sum then rebuilds the values: [1, 3, 3, 7, 2]. Index 3 gets 2 + 5 = 7, and index 4 only gets the +2. This makes each range update O(1).

dsa-complexity:4.prompt: Which problems are naturally solved with prefix sums (possibly plus a hash map)? Select all that apply.
options: Many range-sum queries on a static array
Counting subarrays with sum exactly k
Finding the running median of a data stream
Finding a pivot index where left sum equals right sum
Longest substring without repeating characters
dsa-complexity:4.explanation: Range sums, subarray-sum counting and pivot index all reduce to differences of prefix sums. A running median needs two heaps, and longest unique substring is a sliding window with a set or map.

dsa-complexity:4.prompt: Which statements about prefix techniques are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Prefix XOR answers range-XOR queries, because x ^ x = 0
Range products via prefix products and division break when the array contains zeros
Prefix sums require the input to be sorted
Using a prefix array of length n + 1 with P[0] = 0 removes the special case for ranges starting at index 0
dsa-complexity:4.explanation: Any invertible associative operation works (XOR undoes itself); division can't undo a zero; the leading 0 sentinel simplifies indexing. Prefix sums work on any order: sorting would change which elements are contiguous.

dsa-complexity:4.prompt: After one element of the underlying array changes, a prefix-sum array still answers range sums correctly in O(1) without being rebuilt.
options: True
False
dsa-complexity:4.explanation: Every P[j] after the changed index is now stale, so you must update O(n) entries. For frequent updates, use a Fenwick tree or segment tree.
